analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for workers to form unions and adds real penalties for employers who illegally fire or threaten them.
analysis.headline: The Employee Free Choice Act of 2009 was introduced with 40 Senate cosponsors but never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and it died in the Senate HELP Committee when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the nation's basic labor law in three ways. First, if a majority of workers at a workplace signed cards saying they wanted a union, the government would certify the union directly, skipping the employer-contested secret-ballot election that currently follows. Second, if a newly certified union and the employer could not agree on a first contract after roughly four months, a government mediator and then an arbitrator would impose a binding two-year contract, ending the common tactic of bargaining forever without agreeing. Third, employers who illegally fired or threatened workers trying to organize would owe double back pay plus civil penalties of up to $20,000 per violation, and those cases would get fast-track investigations and court injunctions.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want to join a union, especially in industries like retail, hospitality, healthcare, and manufacturing where organizing drives currently fail because of delay and employer retaliation. Workers gain a faster path to union recognition, real monetary penalties when employers illegally fire or threaten organizers, and a guaranteed first contract instead of endless stalled bargaining. The labor unions that would represent these workers also gain members and revenue, but only if a majority of the workers themselves sign up.

how_it_helps.text: The NLRB would have to certify a union as soon as a majority of employees in a workplace signed authorization cards, eliminating the employer-contested election period during which many workers are pressured or fired.

Employers who illegally fire or threaten pro-union workers during an organizing drive would owe back pay plus double that amount in liquidated damages, and up to $20,000 in civil penalties per willful or repeated violation, instead of the current practice of back pay alone.
Charges of illegal retaliation during organizing drives would get priority investigation and mandatory injunctions, so remedies would arrive in months rather than the years it currently takes.

If a newly certified union and the employer could not reach a first contract, the dispute would go through mediation and then binding arbitration, so employers could no longer simply stall indefinitely to make the union worthless.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that would face union organizing drives, particularly large non-union companies in retail, hospitality, healthcare, and manufacturing. They lose the current election-period window to campaign against a union, face doubled back-pay awards and $20,000-per-violation penalties for illegal retaliation, and risk having a first contract set by an arbitrator if they stall in bargaining. Non-union employers' shareholders bear these costs indirectly through reduced management leverage over labor costs.

drawbacks.text: Under the card-check provision, the NLRB would certify a union based on signed authorization cards alone, with no secret-ballot election, so employees who signed a card under social or union pressure and later changed their mind would have no private vote to reverse course.

If a newly certified union and employer cannot agree on a first contract, a government-appointed arbitration board would impose a binding two-year contract, meaning wages, benefits, and work rules could be set by an arbitrator rather than by either the workers or the employer at the bargaining table.

The new $20,000-per-violation penalties, doubled back pay, and fast-track injunctions apply only to employer misconduct during organizing, not to comparable misconduct by unions, leaving the enforcement rules one-sided.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were real and large for workers who want a union: certification by majority sign-up removes the long, delay-prone election period where most illegal retaliation happens, and doubled back pay plus $20,000 per-violation penalties gave employers an actual reason to obey the law. The costs are also real. Card-check ends the private-ballot election that many employees and union skeptics value, and binding arbitration of first contracts hands wage and benefit decisions to a third party with no vote by either workers or management. The bill's design was contested on those grounds in good faith; it was never debated or amended in committee, so those flaws were never tested against fixes.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced, no one ever brought it to a vote there, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on March 10, 2009 by Senator Kennedy and read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The action history shows no committee markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind after the initial referral.
The bill's last entry in the record is the March 10, 2009 referral; the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill died in committee without coming to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and business groups that opposed easier unionization came out ahead: the bill never advanced past its first-day referral, and the existing system, in which employer-side penalties are minimal and unionization rates kept falling, remained in place. Workers hoping to organize and the unions that would have represented them are worse off.

for.name: Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 10, 2009 and recruited a broad slate of Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 38 of 58 Senate Democrats, plus the Senate's one Independent and one Independent Democrat
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Tom Harkin, Sherrod Brown, Bernie Sanders, and Joe Lieberman.

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Publicly endorsed the bill as a candidate and president, though his administration never prioritized bringing it to the floor.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and allied business groups
against.what_they_did: Ran a sustained public and lobbying campaign against the bill, making it the top legislative priority of the business lobby in 2009.

against.name: Arlen Specter
against.what_they_did: Announced on the Senate floor in March 2009 that he would vote against the bill, denying supporters the 60th vote needed to end debate; he never cosponsored it.

against.name: 40 of 40 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 40 Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill, and it faced certain filibuster without Republican support.

sides.party_line_note: All 40 cosponsors were Democrats or allied independents and not a single Republican signed on, while every Senate Republican opposed it, making support and opposition almost perfectly partisan.

industries.industry: Employers in union-organizing sectors (retail, hospitality, manufacturing, healthcare)
industries.note: The bill removes the long election window in which employers can fight organizing drives, adds real penalties for firing or threatening pro-union workers, and allows an arbitrator to impose a first contract if the company stalls. For consumers, the practical effect is that low-wage workers in these sectors would gain a proven route to higher pay through collective bargaining.

Majority sign-up certification, faster first contracts, and stronger penalties would make organizing dramatically easier and grow union membership and dues. Unlike in many bills, the unions' gain here runs with workers' gain: workers only get a union if a majority of them sign up for one.

A large industry exists to run anti-union campaigns and stretch out certification battles for employers. Card-check certification and fast-track injunctions against retaliation would shrink the demand for those services.
